thread.title: SoftBank: Price Is What You Pay, Asset Supported Value And A Free Option Is What You Get (Part II) - SoftBank Group ADR (OTCMKTS:SFTBY)

author: Gordon Investing
title: SoftBank: Price Is What You Pay, Asset Supported Value And A Free Option Is What You Get (Part II) - SoftBank Group ADR (OTCMKTS:SFTBY)
text:
Note: Due to SoftBank's complexity and SA article length requirements, there are 4 parts to this write-up: Part I - Part I - Executive summary, SoftBank's history, Masayoshi Son's bio and track record . Part II - SoftBank's organizational structure and main holdings. Part III - The Vision Fund and ride sharing investments. Part IV - Debt, risk, intrinsic value, and conclusion.
For the readers who would prefer to see it all at once, you can go to my blog and read all four parts as a whole.
SoftBank Organizational Structure SoftBank ( OTCPK:SFTBY ) is organized as a holding company with a number of subsidiaries. One thing to keep in mind and to avoid confusion: the holding company is called SoftBank Group Corp., while its mobile subsidiary (formerly Vodafone Japan) is SoftBank Corp. in the official documents. For the purpose of this write-up, when I refer to SoftBank or "the Company", the intent is to address SoftBank Group (holding company). That is what the stock ticker SFTBY refers to. If I am discussing the mobile and broadband business, I'm calling it SoftBank Mobile. Throughout this entire analysis, I am using 114 JPY (Japanese yen) to $1 USD exchange rate.
SoftBank Group's corporate website contains basic breakdown of its structure, and is a good place to start.
Although SoftBank is rather complex considering all the equity stakes and subsidiaries, this company is not that difficult to value, namely because most of its large holdings are publicly traded, such as Sprint (NYSE: S ), Yahoo Japan ( OTCPK:YAHOY ), or Alibaba (NYSE: BABA ). I put together a summary table for a quick valuation that includes only the large parts of SoftBank's overall holdings.

Each one of the above entities requires some in-depth discussion. Current, Part II, of my four-part analysis focuses on SoftBank Corp. (Mobile division), Sprint, Yahoo Japan, ARM, Brightstar, Fortress Investment, and Alibaba.
SoftBank Corp.: $45b-$60b SoftBank Group is in the process of spinning off its mobile and broadband business via an IPO, expected to list on the Tokyo Stock Exchange on December 19, 2018. If we take a quick look at SoftBank's main mobile and broadband competitors, we can try to arrive to a reasonable estimate.
Company ADR Stock Symbol 2017 Revenue (b of Yen) 2017 Operating Income (b of Yen) 2017 Total Debt (b of Yen) 2017 Cash & ST Investments (b of Yen) 2017 Revenue (b of $) 2017 Operating Income (b of $) 2017 Total Debt (b of $) 2017 Cash & ST Investments (b of $) Current Mobile Subscribers (millions) Market Cap (b of $) Enterprise Value (b of $) EV/Operating Income NTT Docomo OTCPK:DCMYY ¥4,769 ¥973 ¥162 ¥764 $41.8 $8.5 $1.4 $6.7 77 $93.0 $87.7 9x KDDI OTCPK:KDDIY ¥5,042 ¥963 ¥1,102 ¥201 $44.2 $8.4 $9.7 $1.8 53 $62.0 $69.9 7x SoftBank Corp (H1 2018 x 2) N/A ¥3,590 ¥894 ¥3,246 $31.5 $7.8 $28.5 ??? 43 Est. $31.5 Est. $60 7.7x Source: NTT Docomo Integrated Report 2018, KDDI Financial Statements Summary for the Year Ended March 31, 2018 , and SoftBank Group Consolidated Financial Report for Six Month Period Ended September 30, 2018
Keep in mind, I'm mixing results just a bit in order to account for latest disclosures from SoftBank. For NTT and KDDI, I'm using their results for fiscal year ended in March 2018. For SoftBank Mobile, I'm using first-half results from the latest six-month period, and then just multiplying them by 2 to get a rough estimate for full-year numbers.
Here are some quick observations:
Both NTT and KDDI are larger than SoftBank in terms of revenues, although SoftBank's estimated 2018 operating income is fairly close to the other companies' 2017 operating income. While NTT and KDDI show operating margin around 20%, SoftBank is better at almost 25%. NTT seems to have a very strong balance sheet with excess cash, while KDDI makes as much or more than NTT on a lower subscriber base. SoftBank Mobile is now carrying around 3.2t JPY ($28.5b) total debt and likely that is the debt that IPO'd entity will inherit. We don't know what the net debt will be because we don't know how much cash will go with it. Taking the above numbers under consideration, I arrive at a conservative estimate that SoftBank Mobile IPO's market cap should be around $31.5b, which together with $28.5b in debt, gives it an enterprise value of around $60b. As it turns out, my estimate indeed appears too conservative, and media outlets are reporting that the entire company market capitalization could be worth 7.18t JPY, or $65b. SoftBank Group would sell 1.6b shares (36.9% of total) at 1,500 JPY each, for 2.4t JPY, or $21b in proceeds. This valuation would mean that SoftBank Mobile would trade at a premium to the competition, and its enterprise value would be more than $90b. In this case, I'm happy to be proven incorrect on my valuation, although this Wall Street Journal article is closer to my numbers. It is also citing that potentially high dividend yield (over 5%), may convince retail investors to gobble up SoftBank Mobile's shares. We won't know for sure until December 19, when the new company starts to trade on the TSE.
To provide some cushion on the valuation, I will give SoftBank Mobile $45b valuation, which would result in $16.6b coming to SoftBank Group for parting with almost 37% of its cash cow. On the less conservative end (and, again, I hope this is indeed how things play out), Mobile gets $60b market valuation and the parent entity gets $22b cash infusion.
The timing of the IPO is a bit of unfortunate for SoftBank, considering that both NTT and KDDI are at freshly year low for their stock prices. This is likely the result of the Japanese government pressure on mobile carriers to lower their fees, which could put a dent into everyone's profits.
Giving up a piece of SoftBank Mobile is not to be taken lightly, considering the importance of the Mobile segment to the overall earnings power of the conglomerate, and the amount of debt SoftBank Group has on its balance sheet. Mobile and broadband business accounts for roughly half of the company's operating profit, is critical to servicing parent company's debt, and for keeping its cost of debt low. Once Masa releases this segment out to the public, SoftBank Group won't be able to control its cash any more, and will only be able to count on its dividends. In other words, Masa needs the cash that this segment produces, even if it is outside of the holding company's direct control.
Regardless, I believe that mobile and broadband IPO makes a lot of sense from a big picture and long-term perspective. Masa already moved $28.5 of debt to SoftBank Mobile, and additional $16.6b to $22b cash will help towards deleveraging the parent holding company. There are a couple more positives following this IPO:
Simplification of corporate structure and better alignment to the overall company direction. As my analysis will demonstrate, SoftBank Group market capitalization includes a hefty conglomerate discount. One possible reason for that discount has to do with what kind of investors own SoftBank Group's shares. SoftBank's mobile and broadband unit is a stable, cash-generating business, and it likely attracts the type of shareholders that are looking for stability. To them, the rest of SoftBank Group likely seems more uncertain, too tech-heavy and futuristic, and thus not quite the same type of business as mobile and broadband. Allowing those investors to sell out SoftBank Group and buy into the IPO Mobile segment, should align better the shareholders to Masa's plan for a holding company of technology-driven investments. I am personally always in favor of aligning corporate structures because I believe these activities unlock value that is often readily visible but not realizable under the conglomerate umbrella. I've had some success investing in companies that have done that before, such as when Fiat Chrysler (NYSE: FCAU ) spun off Ferrari (NYSE: RACE ), a company that was vastly different in every aspect when compared to the mothership. By having another publicly traded entity, SoftBank Group gets another vehicle to cash out if servicing or issuing debt becomes problematic or even if Masa determines that owning a mobile/broadband business is not critical to his overall strategy any more. One of the key questions related to the IPO is how the market will react and what will happen to SoftBank Group's share price. If half of operating earnings are about to be IPO'd, then will SFTBY price drop by half or some other significant amount, as shareholders rotate out and new ones buy in? No one knows the answer to this, but if the price drops, I would personally take that as an opportunity to load up and buy even more. If you take a look at the behavior of Fiat Chrysler and Ferrari, both companies had a significant drop post IPO, resulting in some great buying opportunities for investors who took the time to understand these companies rather than follow the market sentiment.
Sprint Corp.: $21.6b SoftBank owns almost 85% of Sprint. At today's market value, that comes out to about $21.6b. Sprint's sizable, almost $40b, debt is non-recourse to SoftBank meaning that even if Sprint goes belly up, SoftBank is not on the hook for any of it. This is important to remember because in SoftBank's financials, Sprint's debt is combined with the other debt that the holding company has. Sprint finances this debt through its own earnings.
I don't want to get too much into Sprint's finances, because it is publicly traded and easy to see. In the last 3 years, Sprint has been improving its operating earnings, but again, due to high debt level, it is currently making enough from operations to simply just service its debt. There are no dividends, and SoftBank is not pulling any cash from it. In terms of assets, aside from hard assets, and subscribers, Sprint also owns an enormous amount of wireless spectrum, which is an important card to play in the upcoming 5G rollout.
When Masa bought the 4 th largest US carrier Sprint in 2012, his original plan was to buy the 3 rd largest, T-Mobile (NASDAQ: TMUS ), then combine the two companies into a formidable competitor and then go after Verizon's (NYSE: VZ ) and AT&T's (NYSE: T ) customers. In a sense he was following similar playbook as when he purchased Vodafone, turned it into SoftBank Mobile, and then went after competition asleep at the wheel. However, US regulatory bodies did not allow for it to happen during the Obama administration. Just a few months ago, another merger attempt has been put in place, this time T-Mobile is proposing to acquire Sprint. Masa would give up control of Sprint and own 27% of the combined company. The FCC is currently reviewing the merger, which will be the deciding factor if it happens or not. I have no way of handicapping the odds of the FCC or Justice Department approving the merger, but it appears that both companies have learned something during their past attempts, and that they are trying to get in front of regulators' concerns.
If the merger takes place, it would be net positive for SoftBank, even though Masa would lose full control of Sprint. Namely, the argument that both Sprint and T-Mobile are making is that upcoming 5G rollout is going to need massive investments, and combination of spectrum, something that neither company can do by itself in order to effectively compete against Verizon and AT&T. The idea for combining these is rather rational, although T-Mobile appears to be in a better financial and operating earnings position, with debt of around $30b, and already making enough from operations to comfortably service the debt. Combining the companies should allow to spread fixed costs over a larger base of customers, and use the extra money to invest in 5G.
Another benefit of the merger has to do with SoftBank Group's balance sheet. Currently, Sprint's debt, almost $40b, is showing on SoftBank's consolidated balance sheet. This debt will magically disappear from it, once SoftBank's stake in the combined Sprint - T-Mobile entity drops to 27%, which is below the 50% threshold requiring consolidated statements. Instead, SoftBank would represent its ownership in the new entity under the equity method of reporting.
"Every Act of Creation is First an Act of Destruction" - Pablo Picasso
Should Sprint/T-Mobile merger happen, and SoftBank Mobile IPO also takes place, SoftBank Group's main business won't be telecom operations any more. Rather it will resemble a holding company with investments across the new tech universe. This is also in line with some of Masa's statements in his recent investor calls, when he stated that 97% of his brain is focused on Singularity and future, as opposed to telecom companies. I think it also illustrates Masa's capacity to move away from what worked in the past and focus on the future. Aligning the structure to reflect the new reality should allow for a more accurate representation of SoftBank for the investment community.
Yahoo Japan Corp.: $7b Yahoo Japan was an early brainchild of Masa. Having taken a 35% in original (US) Yahoo for a $100m in 1996, Masa reasoned that Yahoo should have a Japanese language web search portal, and with a minimal investment of $1.2m, SoftBank owned 60% of the newly formed venture. Unlike US-based Yahoo, which struggled post dot com boom due to relentless competition from Google and Facebook, Yahoo Japan continues to be a dominant web portal in Japan. Its search engine is powered by Google, and the company has a strong advertising brand in Japan, on par with Google.
We could use Yahoo Japan as another example of Masa's ability to make a bet on a future (Yahoo US), then figure how to localize that to Japanese market (Yahoo Japan), and then, instead of sitting on his laurels, he moved to mobile, as Yahoo Japan continued to be relevant to Japanese web and mobile users. As original US based Yahoo mightily struggled, and made one error after another, competitors such as Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) and Facebook (NASDAQ: FB ) ate its lunch. Yahoo Japan however continued to evolve, making bets in mobile before everyone else did, and to this day, remains a powerful player in Japan's web and mobile universe.
In July of this year, Altaba ( AABA ), which is the remaining company that used to be the old Yahoo US, sold around 5% of its Yahoo Japan shares to SoftBank for $2b. Then, Yahoo Japan bought back the same amount of shares from SoftBank. Effectively, this was a tender offer, which allows SoftBank to increase its ownership stake in Yahoo Japan, without reaching in its own pocket for $2b.
Here are some quick observations based on Yahoo Japan's 2018 Year End Financials:
After the tender offer, Yahoo Japan has around 5.2b shares outstanding. SoftBank owns about 48% or 2.5b shares now. Yahoo Japan pays 8.86 yen per share in dividends, thus, before taxes, SoftBank gets some 22b yen in dividends, or $192m per year. The company produces around $2.1b in EBITDA, $1.7b in operating income, and around $1.3b in after tax profit. SoftBank has a claim to around half of that or some $600m. However, the only way for SoftBank to get more of that cash would be through dividends that Yahoo Japan pays out. Dividend ratio is currently around 40%, and it is questionable how much more that can grow for a company that certainly has to invest in technology and other capex in order to stay relevant. Yahoo Japan is debt-free, with a solid cash position of over $5b currently according to the latest financials. It is hard to predict with much certainty exactly how Yahoo Japan fits into Masa's big picture, but I suspect that Yahoo Japan's strong balance sheet can be used to improve SoftBank's own capital structure. The tender that increased SoftBank's stake in Yahoo Japan did not push it over 50%, although it is quite possible that Masa may want to increase the stake to allow him to consolidate cash-rich Yahoo Japan into the SoftBank's balance sheet. After that, the next move could be to use Yahoo Japan's healthy EBITDA and debt-free balance sheet as a guarantee for issuing more SoftBank's debt that Masa can deploy into the next stage companies or deleverage SoftBank. One clue to this can be found on page 24 of the June 30, 2018, Earnings Results Presentation:
Improve EPS of YJ/Achieve efficient rebalancing of the capital structure
I will discuss SoftBank debt later on in this analysis, but one thing is clear - SoftBank's ability to issue debt is approaching limits with the current structure, and the company may be looking at ways to take advantage of some valuable assets in which it has a significant stake, such as Yahoo Japan.
ARM Limited: $24b To date, ARM has been the largest purchase that Masa completed. He bought ARM in 2016 for $32b, and the intent is to use it as a central part of his Singularity strategy.
For those not familiar with ARM, it is important to distinguish it from chip manufacturers. ARM does not have manufacturing facilities and it does not produce chips, unlike Intel (NASDAQ: INTC ) and AMD (NASDAQ: AMD ). Instead, ARM licenses its design and technology to other companies, such as Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), for example, which then builds its own chips on top of the ARM design for their next iPhone CPU. In a sense, ARM is a company able to leverage its strong intellectual property and capability of its engineering organization to dominate a complex field such as chip design. Because it does not need fixed assets for manufacturing, ARM operates with a capital-light business model. On the front end, ARM charges its customers a fee to create chip designs, and on the back end, ARM gets a small royalty from each chip the customer sells. The royalties are often just cents per device, but considering how many ARM licensed chips are out there, this revenue stream continues to increase. This makes more sense when we start to think of chips not just in our phones and computers, but also in many more everyday devices. For example, an average new car manufactured today contains some 500 ARM licensed chips. Below diagram from ARM's Q2/FY2018 Roadshow Slides illustrates how ARM's model works.
One of the keys to ARM's success lies within its entrenched ecosystem. Effectively, due to its architecture and widespread use, ARM dominates chips for mobile and IoT devices. Its clients build their own devices around this architecture, and thus there is a high switching cost that assures clients won't easily defect to a competitor or decide to make chips from scratch internally. Developing a chip infrastructure is as complex as it sounds, and rather than doing it on their own, clients farm this out to ARM for about 1/10th of the cost it would take to do it in house. ARM continues to make advances in low power management, security, and connectivity, while dropping down overall cost. The cost advantage is a very important aspect here, and ARM continues to offer more functionality for less cost, which keeps its customers happy and ARM entrenched.
As below chart shows, there were around 10 billion ARM chips shipped back in 2012. Six years later, in 2017, there were more than 20 billion shipped. With average yearly growth rate of more than 15%, this trend is expected to continue.
Source: Author based on ARM and SoftBank financial disclosures
The graph below illustrates that growth in revenues and profits at ARM were mostly following the number of chips licensed. But then, something changed when Masa got involved. He wanted ARM to invest a lot more into R&D, to double its workforce, and get ready for the future. Had ARM remained a public company, this would have been a difficult task because stock market would not react too well to a sudden drop in profits and huge cost increases. But within SoftBank, this approach is a lot more palatable.
Source: Page 34 of ARM Q1 2018 Roadshow Slides
When Masa bought ARM in 2016 for $32b, at a 40% premium, the company had only $1.5b of revenue and $450m profit. So the multiples were staggering. At the time the deal was announced, SoftBank shares dropped 10% on the news, with analysts scratching their heads, and wondering how would SoftBank, which at the time was mostly a telecom type company (see SoftBank Mobile and Sprint above), benefit from a chip designer. Little did they know, that ARM purchase was yet another chess move Masa made in order to pivot SoftBank towards Singularity, and away from what worked in the past. ARM was also the key to the Vision Fund, whose creation followed once ARM purchase was complete. In fact, in order to satisfy SoftBank's own contribution requirements to the Vision Fund, Masa placed 25% of ARM into the Vision Fund. Thus, only 75% of it is still purely owned by SoftBank.
For the purpose of this analysis, I value ARM at the same price Masa bought it, $32b, minus the $8b that SoftBank contributed into the Vision Fund, resulting in $24b ARM current value. In my opinion, ARM could be worth multiple of this price. Not just because IoT market is expected to continue to grow exponentially and ARM is right in the middle of it, but also, in the hands of Masa, ARM is a strategic asset, critical to the entire Singularity execution for SoftBank.
If we take a look at how old industries and many competitors toppled when products and services were reinvented, such as with iPhone, ride-sharing services, or online shopping, one constant is always there. None of the changes could happen if it wasn't for the continuous advances in microchips. ARM plays the central role at SoftBank and as new industries span, from efficient GPS farming, to self-driving cars, to fully connected cities, robotics, and so many uses for Artificial Intelligence, there will be more and more chips needed. These chips will have to be increasingly sophisticated, pack additional power, use less energy, connect via the cloud, and have faster time to market. ARM is the leader in all those areas and with SoftBank support, it is expected to only accelerate what it can deliver and how it can anticipate where the industry is heading next.
Besides selling more chips, Masa gets an added benefit from ARM, and that is advanced glimpse into IoT future. The key aspect of chip design is that it needs to be done well in advance of actual use, often 2 years ahead. As ARM owns some 95% of the mobile chip market design, and as it expands as the leader in IoT, at the time when customers place orders for these chips, Masa can gauge where the demand will be a couple of years in advance. Then he can use this first hand intelligence data to accordingly invest in those companies or new industries that are created, as long as they fit his overall vision. That is something that his competitors cannot readily access.
Brightstar and Fortress Investment Group: $4b I won't spend much time analyzing these two entities. Brightstar is a low margin mobile distribution/trade in/insurance business that SoftBank initially invested in 2013. According to this Reuters article , SoftBank is looking to sell this asset and the numbers being discussed are around $1b.
At the end of 2017, SoftBank purchased alternative asset manager Fortress Investment Group with $36b in assets under management. As discussed in this press release , SoftBank paid $3.3b in cash for it. I will give it a current value of $3b.
Alibaba Group: $89b - $110.8b When Masa invested in Alibaba in 2000, during the dot com crash, Alibaba was an obscure Chinese startup. Masa stated himself that Jack Ma showed up to the meeting without the business plan, and, at the time, Alibaba's business offerings were vastly different than today. However, while meeting with Ma, Masa quickly realized that he had an exceptional potential. Masa ended up investing $20m for a 37% of Alibaba, and only because Jack Ma wouldn't agree to give up 50% for $40m which Masa was proposing. Today, that 37% is pared down to 29% and according to Alibaba's current market capitalization of $382b, SoftBank's stake is worth almost $111b. SoftBank is the largest Alibaba shareholder, and Masa sits on the board.
Alibaba is one of a handful of dominant companies in the second largest economy in the world. China's economy is built upon small and medium manufacturing businesses and trading type companies. In this ecosystem, Alibaba plays a central role as it connects all these manufacturers with millions of Chinese and international buyers. If you are a producer from China or buyer from the US or another country, the most convenient and safe way to find your product or a buyer for your product is to use Alibaba. Producers have to pay annual fee, security deposit, and a commission when selling products.
But that's not all Alibaba does in China. There are a number of other dominant businesses owned by Alibaba, such as TMall (for connecting foreign producers with Chinese retail customers), Taobao (kind of like Chinese Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ) or eBay (NASDAQ: EBAY )(for Chinese companies selling to Chinese retail customers). Then there is Alipay, which is a must in China because most of the businesses don't accept credit cards - even a corner fruit vendor uses a bar code which customer scans and payment is processed at a fraction of a price what a credit card company may charge. In a sense, Alipay (which has more than 50% market share) and competing product WeChat from Tencent ( OTCPK:TCEHY ), together own mobile payment system in a country of 1.4b people. Alibaba owns 33% of Alipay, which will eventually go public at a possible $100b+ valuation, according to this Wall Street Journal article . Also, Alibaba is the largest player in cloud services in China, and it owns equity stakes in a number of other businesses.
Alibaba continues to grow at a staggering pace due to its entrenched economic ecosystem which acts as a toll bridge in the Chinese economy, and also because of the favorable demographic trends in the markets it operates. As hundreds of millions of Chinese still lack the Internet access, the runway for growth is there and the company just needs to execute.

Just in September of this year, Alibaba announced that Jack Ma, who is only 54, and worth some $24b, not including Ant Financial, is retiring from his executive chairman position at Alibaba to focus on his philanthropic efforts. Back in 2013, Jack Ma stepped down as the company CEO. He is supposed to remain a board member and still own more than 6% stake in the company. Clearly, the market was not too thrilled about these news, as Alibaba stock continues to drop following the announcement. Possibly, the investors are concerned if Chinese government orchestrated this change, if they tightened control over this company, and if Alibaba can continue on its growth path without its founder at the helm. A trade war with the US certainly does not help the case as the Chinese stock market continues to drop due to geopolitical and trade issues with the US.
With its overall size and importance for the Chinese economy, Alibaba could be considered a monopoly under a close watch and likely protection from Chinese government. That can be a two-edged sword, but as long as the company does not veer too far from the wishes of the party rulers, it is likely to continue to enjoy its top position.
By the virtue of owning such a large chunk of Alibaba, a big portion of SoftBank's own value is derived from Alibaba. Although no one can predict with certainty where the US - China tensions may lead, I am of opinion that self-interest will govern the overall outcome. The US and China have too many critically important dependencies, and a solution reasonable to all sides should be achievable. If that is the case, current tariffs are just a bump in the road, and long term, Alibaba will stay on its path of growth, and with it, SoftBank's ownership value will continue to increase.
SoftBank's Alibaba Ownership Details There is a fly in SoftBank's Alibaba soup that requires some discussion. When it comes to owning strategic assets in China, such as technology or banking companies, for example, the Chinese law bars foreigners to directly own shares and exercise control over those companies. However, Chinese companies still want outside capital, and to get around that, they set up offshore entities, called Variable Interest Entities (VIE), usually in tax havens, that have contractual claims on the Chinese tech companies' earnings. These offshore entities then sell shares in the Western stock exchanges, allowing participation, but not ownership in the businesses. This article does a good job explaining it in more detail, as well as this one .
Here is a quick summary of Alibaba's corporate governance as explained in its website . The company has 11 directors in total. Out of these 11 seats, simple majority, or 6 directors, are nominated by the Alibaba Partnership , essentially the original founders of the company, including Jack Ma, and other key executives, a total of 36 people. The Partnership currently gives 1 of its 6 seats to SoftBank, under the condition that SoftBank holds at least 15% of the shares, with the expectation that it would vote in line with the Alibaba Partnership nominees. Masa has been the director in this seat since 2000.
What this means practically is that SoftBank's stake in Alibaba is not the same as its stake in Sprint or Yahoo Japan. Although SoftBank owns almost third of the shares traded on the Western exchanges, its ability to impact how Alibaba runs its business is rather limited.
Likewise, the contractual obligations between the VIE and Alibaba are only enforceable in the Chinese courts and could be impacted by political or other influence rather than the letter of the law.
In my opinion, the above structure creates some uncertainty as to the real value SoftBank's Alibaba stake. The Chinese government would be smart not to mess with the VIE structures if they desire outside capital. Frankly, the setup seems lopsided to the benefit of the Chinese and it is the Western investors who are taking a leap of faith that trading pieces of paper on the Western stock markets will be honored by the Chinese courts. If the geopolitical tensions grow, who is to say that the Chinese won't decide that VIE is not enforceable? Or what if the Chinese tech giants become so big that the Chinese government simply determines that it wouldn't want to share the riches with the foreigners?
Admittedly, these and many other potential scenarios are hard to handicap. I believe that Alibaba is poised to continue to dominate in China, and with it, its market value is more likely to be rising over the long term. Current market value of Alibaba's SoftBank owned shares is $111b. If there is a 20% chance that in the future SoftBank would need to write off part of Alibaba's value due to the above-mentioned corporate governance and political risk, that would still give it some $89b in current value.
This concludes Part II. In Part III, I will discuss the Vision Fund and SoftBank's ride-sharing investments.
